name: Example: Finding the Derivative of a Polar Curve Given the Derivatives With Respect To X and Y
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059545/assets/a0eb20697f72b1ec5f06cc1ebfa4ba364c1023c915950b64cfab2367964db928.png)

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r = 2^{\theta}$ (shown above) given that

$$
y'(\theta) = 2^{\theta}(\ln 2\sin\theta+ \cos\theta), \qquad
x'(\theta) = 2^{\theta}(\ln 2\cos\theta-\sin\theta) .
$$
worked_solution:
To find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ we use the rule for differentiating parametric equations:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{2}^{\theta }(\operatorname{ln}⁡2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{{2}^{\theta }(\operatorname{ln}⁡2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{ln}⁡2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$
